content: MTA1, or Metastasis-associated protein 1, is a protein encoded by the MTA1 gene in humans. It is the founding member of the MTA family of genes. While MTA1 is primarily localized in the nucleus, it is also distributed in extra-nuclear compartments. This protein is a component of several chromatin remodeling complexes, including the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylation (NuRD) complex. MTA1 regulates gene expression by acting as a coregulator, integrating DNA-interacting factors to modulate gene activity. It plays roles in both normal physiological functions and cancer cell biology. Notably, MTA1 is one of the most upregulated proteins in human cancers and is associated with cancer progression, aggressive phenotypes, and poor prognosis in cancer patients. MTA1 was first cloned in 1994 by Toh, Pencil, and Nicholson as a differentially expressed gene in a highly metastatic rat breast cancer cell line. Its role in chromatin remodeling was inferred from the presence of MTA1 polypeptides in the NuRD complex. The first direct target of the MTA1-NuRD complex was identified as estrogen receptor alpha (ERα). The MTA1 protein is 715 or 703 amino acids long and is encoded by one of three genes in the MTA family. In humans, it is located on chromosome 14q32, while in mice, it is found on chromosome 12F. The human MTA1 gene spans approximately 51 kilobases and contains 21 exons, but only eight spliced transcripts have open reading frames, coding for six proteins and two polypeptides. The remaining transcripts are non-coding long RNAs, some of which retain intron sequences. In mice, the Mta1 gene produces three protein-coding transcripts and three non-coding RNA transcripts. Among human MTA1 variants, two spliced variants are characterized: the ZG29p variant, derived from the C-terminal MTA1, is 251 amino acids long with a molecular weight of 29 kDa, and the MTA1s variant, generated from alternative splicing of a middle exon followed by a frame-shift, is 430 amino acids long with a molecular weight of 47 kDa. MTA1 contains conserved domains such as BAH (Bromo-Adjacent Homology), ELM2 (egl-27 and MTA1 homology), SANT (SWI, ADA2, N-CoR, TFIIB-B), and a GATA-like zinc finger. Its C-terminal divergent region includes an Src homology 3-binding domain, acidic regions, and nuclear localization signals. These domains enable MTA1 to interact with modified or unmodified histone and non-histone proteins, participate in chromatin remodeling, and modulate gene transcription. MTA1 undergoes multiple post-translational modifications, including acetylation on lysine 626, ubiquitination on lysines 182 and 626, sumoylation on lysine 509, and methylation on lysine 532. Structural insights into MTA1 domains have been derived from studies involving complexes with HDAC1 or RbAp48 subunits of the NuRD complex. The MTA1s variant lacks a nuclear localization sequence but contains a novel 33-amino-acid sequence in its C-terminal region, which harbors a nuclear receptor-binding motif (LXXLL) that allows interaction with estrogen receptor alpha or other type I nuclear receptors. The ZG29p variant represents the C-terminal MTA1 with two proline-rich SH3-binding sites. MTA1 expression is regulated by transcriptional and non-transcriptional mechanisms. It is influenced by growth factors, growth factor receptors, oncogenes, environmental stress, ionizing radiation, inflammation, and hypoxia. Transcription of MTA1 is stimulated by transcription factors such as c-Myc, SP1, CUTL1 homeodomain, NF-κB, HSF1, HIF-1α, and the Clock/BMAL1 complex, while it is inhibited by p53. Non-genomic mechanisms of MTA1 expression include post-transcriptional regulation, such as ubiquitination by the RING-finger ubiquitin-protein ligase COP1, interaction with tumor suppressor ARF, or regulation by microRNAs like miR-30c, miR-661, and miR-125a-3p. The functions of MTA1 are regulated by its post-translational modifications, interactions with other regulatory proteins and chromatin remodeling machinery, and modulation of target gene expression through components of the NuRD complex, including HDACs. MTA1 suppresses the transcription of genes such as BRCA1, PTEN, p21WAF, Gαi2, SMAD7, NR4A1, and SIX3, as well as repressing BCL11B and E-cadherin expression. Conversely, MTA1 acts as a dual coregulatory protein by stimulating the transcription of genes like Stat3, BCAS3, FosB, Pax5, TG2, MyD88, p14/p19ARF, tyrosine hydroxylase, Cry1, SUMO2, Wnt1, and rhodopsin. It achieves this by releasing transcriptional inhibition mediated by homeodomain protein SIX3. MTA1 interacts with ERα and coregulatory factors such as MAT1, MICoA, NRIF3, and LMO4, inhibiting ER transactivation activity. Additionally, MTA1 deacetylates target proteins like p53 and HIF, modulating their transactivation functions. MTA1 may also influence target gene expression through the microRNA network, as MTA1 knockdown alters the levels of miR-210, miR-125b, miR-194, miR-103, and miR-500. MTA1 modulates the expression of target genes by acting as a corepressor or coactivator. Its target and effector pathways regulate cellular functions in both normal and cancer cells. Physiological functions of MTA1 include its role in the brain through interactions with DJ1 and endophilin-3, regulation of rhodopsin expression in the murine eye, modulation of circadian rhythm via interactions with the CLOCK-BMAL1 complex and stimulation of Cry transcription, involvement in heart development through MTA1-FOG2 interaction, and roles in mammary gland development, spermatogenesis, immunomodulation, liver regeneration following hepatic injury, differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into the osteogenic axis, and DNA damage response. In cancer cells, MTA1 and its downstream effectors regulate genes and pathways involved in transformation, invasion, survival, angiogenesis, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, metastasis, DNA damage response, and hormone independence in breast cancer.
